The answer is complicated.

First let's consider ductile materials - those that deform without fracturing. Think aluminum foil. In ductile materials, two dislocations can get stuck as they try to pass through each other. This makes the material harder to deform. When a material like this has been extensively deformed, it becomes harder to deform further. This is called work hardening. Materials like steel are commonly deformed (forging) to create a tangle of dislocations and make them stronger. This is why wrenches often advertise that they are forged, because they are stronger than wrenches made from slowly cooled steel that has fewer dislocations.

Second let's consider non-ductile (brittle) materials like diamond. The region around a dislocation often has irregular chemical bond angles that take less energy to break. In a material like this, the dislocation makes it weaker. The turbine blades in high-performance jet engines are laboriously grown from single crystals of metal for this reason.

There are two kinds of universe you can live in. One where the maximal speed of information transfer is infinite, and one where the maximal speed of information transfer is finite. We live in the second kind, and we call that limit c. Light in vacuum happens to travel at that speed limit, which is how we discovered it, which is why we call it "the speed of light in vacuum", even though it is a property inherent to the universe and not something strongly connected to light itself.

If there is a limit to the speed of information transfer, that means that when two places are far apart, it will take some time before an event in one place can affect an event in another place. This is basic causality: causes precede effects. Now with this speed limit in place, you will notice some weird effects. As you move faster and faster, the order of certain events will start to change. Some events will happen before others depending on how fast and in what direction you are traveling, but only when those events are too far apart to influence each other. When one event can influence another, their time order is fixed. And the only way to reverse that would be to go faster than light. Which you can't.

The fact that this speed limit is constant for all observers has some other weird effects. It turns out that if you build a light clock, the very act of watching that clock from a moving perspective will make it run slower. This is not a measurement error or a particular effect of specifically that kind of clock, this applies to all movement and all clocks. But if that speed limit is supposed to be constant, and time can slow down, what does that imply? It implies that space must collapse to accomodate. A signal traveling at the speed of light will always travel at the speed of light, because the amount of time dilation (slowing down) is exactly compensated by the amount of length contraction (space shortening).

Time dilation and length contraction are weird concepts to wrap your head around, but they are very real. Just remember that there is no absolute time or space, that all measurements of these are relative. When you look at the universe from one single perspective, everything makes perfect sense.
